newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rwanda says will let aid through, rebels talking.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda says will let aid through, rebels talking.

text.p: Rwanda has given permission for aid to be delivered from its territory to a million refugees in eastern Zaire, but aid agencies said on Sunday they were still negotiating with rebels over the border for a similar deal.
The decision was a major climbdown by Rwanda, which had previously insisted aid should only be distributed inside the tiny Central African nation to returning refugees.

Samantha Boulton, spokeswoman for the medical charity Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF- Doctors without Frontiers), told Reuters that Rwanda gave its permission on Sunday to a consortium of non-governmental agencies.

But talks with the rebel Alliance for Democratic Forces of Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), who control most of the eastern Zaire's border area including the city of Goma, were still limping on, she said.
"Rwanda has given us permission to leave Rwanda with food and medical aid for the refugees in eastern Zaire," Boulton said.

"But we are still negotiating with the rebels for a similar deal to allow us to reach the refugees. Our trucks are still stuck in the no man's land but we are hopeful a deal would be reached late today or early on Monday."

Boulton said the situation was particularly desperate for some 750,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees trapped in the fighting outside Goma, many of them in the vast refugee camp of Mugunga where armed Hutu rebels are holding out.
She said the United Nations, on the other hand, was seeking permission from the governments of both Rwanda and Zaire to deliver food and medicines to the refugees.

Permission for the aid to reach dying and starving refugees caame ahead of a visit to Kigali by European Commissioner Emma Bonino, who diplomats said would try to persuade Rwanda to talk the rebels into opening a humanitarian corridor.
"This is an effort outside the United Nations, which has failed to come up with a clear response to the crisis in Zaire," one diplomat told Reuters.
"She will be asking Rwanda to use her influence on the rebels to get them to open up a corridor so aid can reach the refugees and so that they also return home," said another.
Zaire accuses Rwanda of backing the rebels but Kigali strongly denies the accusations, saying the rebellion in eastern Zaire was an internal matter.
The World Food Programme (WFP) said it would send an assessment mission into eastern Zaire to check on humanitarian needs and security.
"We will be sending in a team, hopefully today, to assess the humanitarian needs in eastern Zaire and also check on security," WFP spokesman Francis Mwanza told Reuters.

The U.N. Security Council agreed on Saturday that a multinational relief force should be deployed, but not how or when -- and gave U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali another 11 days to come up with a "concept" for the force.
Aid agencies say hungry and thirsty Burundian and Rwandan Hutus must be helped wherever they are, on the mountainsides or barren lava fields of inhospitable eastern Zaire.
The Rwandan refugees fled to Zaire after the genocide of up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994. Hutu gunmen who led the slaughter are with them, and still armed.
